Building a larger quantum computer is not simply a matter of putting more qubits on a chip. Eventually, engineers also have to confront everything connected to them.

In today’s superconducting quantum computers, much of the electronics generating control signals sits at room temperature. Those signals travel through cables into a dilution refrigerator and down through successive temperature stages to qubits operating at temperatures measured in millikelvins. As the number of qubits rises, so does that classical infrastructure.

“The cryostat primarily cools wiring,” Oleg Mukhanov, co-founder and CSO of quantum-control company SEEQC, told EE Times. The problem is not just the physical number of cables. Each provides a path for heat into the cryostat and may require connectors, filters, attenuators, and thermalization at different temperature stages. Additional lines can be required for functions such as tunable couplers and frequency adjustment.

Connectors can fail during repeated cooling cycles. Analog control pulses can also become distorted as they travel from room-temperature waveform generators through the signal chain, Mukhanov said, requiring engineers to compensate by pre-distorting the signals. Moreover, magnetic control signals can introduce crosstalk between neighboring devices.

One increasingly attractive answer is therefore to move more of the classical electronics closer to the quantum processor. Researchers, including MIT professor William Oliver, have examined how cryogenic packaging, signal delivery, and control infrastructure will need to evolve as superconducting-qubit systems grow.

SEEQC has already demonstrated one version of that approach. In a Nature Electronics paper published in March, researchers integrated single-flux-quantum, or SFQ, control electronics, and qubits in a multichip module. Digital demultiplexing allowed control pulses to be distributed among multiple qubits rather than maintaining a one-to-one relationship between control lines and qubits. The researchers reported single-qubit fidelities above 99%, reaching 99.9%.

What electronics belong in the cold?

Moving electronics into the refrigerator, however, raises another problem: what kind of electronics should go there? Cryogenic CMOS has the advantage of decades of semiconductor development behind it. It can provide sophisticated digital, analog, mixed-signal, and memory functions. But pushing CMOS to the performance levels needed for fast qubit control and readout increases power consumption.

“You can make cryogenic CMOS circuits really low power,” S-Transistors co-founder and CEO Heorhii Bohuslavskyi told EE Times. “But if you want to maintain the performance level required for qubits, power dissipation will be high.”

That tradeoff becomes increasingly important deeper inside the cryostat, where available cooling power falls sharply with temperature. Cooling power becomes increasingly scarce as temperatures fall, making dissipation particularly important for electronics placed close to the QPU.

Superconducting SFQ electronics offer almost the opposite tradeoff. Josephson-junction-based circuits can operate extremely quickly with very low energy consumption and are well suited to digital processing. But Bohuslavskyi argued that conventional two-terminal Josephson junctions offer less flexibility for analog, mixed-signal, memory, and other functions.

That gap is what newly formed Finnish startup S-Transistors wants to exploit.

The VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland spinout announced a €2.6 million pre-seed round in August to develop integrated circuits based on superconducting transistors.

Rather than a conventional two-terminal Josephson junction, S-Transistors uses a planar Josephson junction structure equipped with a third gate terminal. The gate can electrically change the properties of the superconducting channel, allowing engineers to control parameters such as critical current and Josephson inductance without relying on local magnetic fields or heating.

The ambition, according to Bohuslavskyi, is to combine the versatility of semiconductor transistors with the low dissipation of superconducting electronics. “We believe that you could really take the very best from both worlds and combine them in one solid-state device,” he said.

Ultimately, S-Transistors envisions what Bohuslavskyi calls a “milli-Kelvin temperature quantum motherboard,” containing much of the I/O, signal routing, control, readout, and eventually other electronics needed around a QPU.

Start with the wires

The company’s first target is considerably narrower. S-Transistors plans to develop superconducting transistor-based time- and frequency-domain multiplexers and demultiplexers, with initial products targeted for 2027. These would allow multiple signals to share connections, reducing the number of physical lines entering the coldest parts of the quantum computer.

That attacks the same bottleneck SEEQC targets with SFQ-based demultiplexing, though with a different device architecture.

Mukhanov said he knows the S-Transistors team and sees potential value in their approach, particularly where different cryogenic technologies have to communicate. “I view their work as very useful and as something that can potentially be deployed,” he said, describing superconducting transistors as a possible “augmentation technology.”

One potential role, he said, would be interfacing superconducting circuits with cryo-CMOS. SFQ circuits, for example, do not offer the same dense memory capabilities as CMOS.

Bohuslavskyi said he sees a larger eventual role. He believes superconducting transistors could take on functions across analog and mixed-signal electronics, routing, control, and memory. But he also expects future quantum-control systems to be heterogeneous. “There will be places for all kinds of different technologies,” he said, including cryo-CMOS and SFQ.

The result may therefore be less a competition to choose one cryogenic electronics technology than an effort to determine which technology belongs at each temperature and at each point in the control stack.

From transistor to integrated circuit

S-Transistors still has a substantial gap to cross. The company said its technology has achieved about 98% device yield on 150-mm wafers and is transitioning toward 200-mm processing. But demonstrating individual superconducting transistors at wafer scale is different from building complex, reliable integrated circuits.

Bohuslavskyi readily acknowledged that distinction. Circuit-level power dissipation and performance figures for the company’s planned multiplexers remain estimates that still have to be experimentally validated.

Another challenge looks surprisingly familiar to anyone from the conventional semiconductor industry: design tools. S-Transistors is developing compact device models and a process design kit so that superconducting transistor circuits can eventually be designed using industrial EDA techniques. Without those tools, Bohuslavskyi said, circuit development risks becoming “a bunch of physicists drawing on the whiteboard and trying to transfer it onto silicon.”

That transition—from promising device physics to repeatable circuit design and manufacturing—may prove as important as the transistor itself.

Meanwhile, the scaling problem S-Transistors is targeting will not disappear if qubit counts continue to rise. Larger fault-tolerant systems will require not only more control signals, but also rapid readout and continuous quantum error correction.

Mukhanov argued that some of that processing will eventually need to happen close to the QPU rather than sending every measurement back to room-temperature electronics. Local processing could reduce both latency and the volume of data traveling out of the refrigerator.

Quantum computing’s next scaling challenge, in other words, may increasingly lie outside the qubits themselves.

Getting more electronics into the cold is one part of the answer. Building electronics capable of doing useful work there without consuming the cooling budget may be the harder part.

Canada’s Semiconductor Council (CSC) is calling on the country’s federal government to make semiconductors an explicit pillar of its recently announced AI strategy.

In a position paper, CSC argues that ambitions for sovereign AI cannot be achieved without a stronger domestic semiconductor foundation.

Paul Slaby, CSC managing director, said Canada’s “AI for All” strategy correctly identifies dependence on foreign chip manufacturing as a strategic vulnerability, but it stops short of treating semiconductors as a formal policy priority. “Sovereign AI requires sovereign silicon,” he said in an interview with EE Times.

He said the strategy is incomplete without a reinforced semiconductor foundation, but rather than seek new major spending programs, the CSC policy paper wants companies to have better access to existing funding and procurement mechanisms already tied to AI development. “The funding vehicles already exist,” Slaby said. “It’s about letting Canadian industry plug into them.”

Among them are the AI Compute Access Fund, the BDC LIFT Fund, and the Canadian Tech Growth Fund.

Slaby said this access should focus on areas where Canada already has strengths, including photonics, compound semiconductors, chip design, and advanced packaging.

More notably, CSC explicitly rejects the idea that Canada should try to compete directly with the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturers. “This is not a call to rival Nvidia or the frontier model race,” Slaby said, adding that Canada’s advantage is brain power, not cash outlay.

Procurement is a central theme of the CSC position paper; it notes Canada’s AI strategy envisions substantial growth in sovereign compute capacity, creating demand for hardware worth billions of dollars. The council argues that spending should be used to strengthen domestic capabilities whenever feasible.

Slaby said there’s an opportunity to put more Canadian semiconductor content into sovereign cloud infrastructure and strengthen the parts of the semiconductor value chain where the country already has world-class expertise and existing assets.

Among those are Canadian Photonics Fabrication Centre (CPFC), which was recently spun off from the National Research Council in Ottawa, advanced packaging capabilities in Bromont, Quebec, and a growing ecosystem of chip design companies. The CSC paper also notes that Canadian optical interconnect technologies are already incorporated into products shipped by global firms including Nvidia and AMD.

Slaby said CSC is promoting a “build, partner, and buy,” message, which is also in line with the Canadian government’s Defense Industrial Strategy (DIS). He said this means building domestic capability where Canada is strong, partnering with trusted allies where necessary, and buying what cannot be built domestically. He added that sovereign compute investments should be used to strengthen Canadian semiconductor capabilities throughout the technology stack.

Slaby highlighted the FABrIC program as one that should continue to receive support from the federal government. Managed by CMC Microsystems, it was established to provide financial and technical resources, mentorship, and training for semiconductor businesses, engineers, and scientists in Canada to help them commercialize their technologies.

It aligns with CSC’s view that Canada should focus on its strengths. FABrIC provides resources to help create new manufacturing processes for compound semiconductors, quantum technologies, photonics, and microelectromechanical systems.

In a news release, CMC said Canada’s AI strategy reflects priorities many organizations across the ecosystem have been advancing for years. “We are encouraged to see a national framework that supports applied innovation and creates the conditions needed for AI adoption at scale,” CMC president and CEO Gordon Harling said in the statement.

The news release noted that FABrIC’s focus on advancing domestic capabilities in semiconductor design and manufacturing aligns well with the AI strategy by supporting the development of advanced semiconductor and intelligent system technologies, enabling AI‑ready hardware and edge intelligent products that strengthen domestic capability, and supporting made‑in‑Canada innovation.

FABrIC also has a significant training and upskilling component to develop highly qualified personnel through access to advanced tools, infrastructure, and experiential learning, supporting workforce readiness for AI‑enabled systems and advanced computing.

Slaby sees training as particularly important and said the CSC wants semiconductor skills to be recognized within federal talent programs. Talent is one of Canada’s biggest advantages, he said, and the country must continue training and retaining semiconductor talent domestically.

In the meantime, CSC is continuing efforts to build relationships internationally. It recently wrapped up trade mission of Canadian companies to the U.K., including London and Southampton, with a delegation attending the TechWorks Semiconductors to Systems Summit 2026 in London at the end of August.

data.title: The Security AI That Learns the Language of Movement
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Most security AI is trained to recognize something specific—an intrusion, a weapon, a fall, a fight, or another predefined event. But public safety threats do not always arrive in familiar forms, and collecting enough labeled examples of every dangerous behavior is impractical.

Hamed Tabkhi, an associate professor at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte (UNC Charlotte), is taking a different approach. Rather than teaching AI to recognize every possible threat, his team is teaching it what normal human movement looks like in a particular environment. The system can then learn how those movements are likely to continue and flag behavior that departs sufficiently from what it expects.

“We are building an LLM for movements,” Tabkhi told EE Times.

The analogy is not literal, as the system is not a large language model, but the underlying idea is similar: A language model learns relationships between tokens and predicts what’s likely to come next. Across several research projects, Tabkhi’s group has developed ways to turn human poses and movements into compact representations that AI models can use to learn patterns over time.

Edge AI on existing CCTV

Tabkhi’s system is designed to work with existing CCTV installations rather than requiring organizations to replace their cameras. A processing device sits inside the closed network and taps video streams from selected IP cameras.

The incoming pixels are analyzed on the fly, but the AI does not need faces, clothing, skin color, or other identifying information to analyze behavior. Instead, the research converts human activity into representations of motion over time and space.

“We just look at the motions and movements,” Tabkhi said. He described the resulting information as motion heat maps or motion tokens.

A 2024 paper from Tabkhi and colleagues introduced a transformer architecture called SPARTA that tokenizes pose information across space and time, allowing the model to capture both the configuration of the body and how that configuration changes. Subsequent work included Shopformer, a transformer-based AI framework developed by Tabkhi’s group for detecting shoplifting from human pose sequences rather than raw video.

Their system does not need to know who a person is to reason about how that person is moving.

The software runs locally on off-the-shelf Nvidia Jetson edge GPU platforms installed inside the CCTV network. Tabkhi said a Jetson-based processing device can connect to multiple cameras without requiring fundamental changes to the existing video infrastructure.

That makes the architecture a form of edge AI. Instead of continuously sending camera streams to a remote cloud service for analysis, the system can process movement locally and generate anomaly alerts close to where the video originates.

For Tabkhi, retrofitting existing infrastructure is important. Cameras are already widespread in campuses, city centers, retailers, and other public environments. “Our AI is a complementary layer,” he said.

The work is supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF), including through the ongoing NSF Civic Innovation Challenge, which enables the team to deploy and evaluate the technology in multiple real-world pilots across Charlotte’s city center.

Learning what’s ‘normal’

The more radical departure is in how the system decides something is suspicious. Traditional supervised AI starts with predefined classes. If developers want a model to recognize shoplifting, for example, they typically need examples of shoplifting behavior and labels telling the system what those examples represent.

Tabkhi argued that this model is poorly suited to many public-safety problems because abnormal events are rare, diverse, and dependent on context. His group instead treats video anomaly detection as an open-ended problem in which the AI learns normal behavior and searches for departures from it.

After deployment, a model can adapt to the environment in which it operates. A coffee shop, university campus, retail store, or intersection each have different patterns of normal behavior.

“The system learns by itself, so it can adjust itself to the unique environment,” Tabkhi said. “You can move this system to any environment, and it’s going to learn the normal behavior of that environment.”

Prediction is one way the researchers have explored that problem. Their TSGAD model—short for two-stream graph-improved anomaly detection—combines learned representations of human movement with trajectory prediction, using differences between expected and observed motion to help identify unusual behavior.

Tabkhi put the principle more simply: “We always try to predict the next motion.”

Retail security provides practical proving ground. Tabkhi’s group has increasingly treated shoplifting as an anomaly-detection problem rather than simply another image-classification task. Its PoseLift work created a privacy-preserving dataset from real retail environments, representing shoppers through pose information while preserving behavioral signals relevant to shoplifting.

Shopformer then applied a transformer specifically to pose sequences for shoplifting detection. More recent research pushes the idea toward continuous real-world deployment.

In a 2026 paper, the researchers describe a dataset collected across multiple cameras in an operating U.S. retail store, supplemented with actual and staged shoplifting incidents. They also address a major deployment problem: A store does not remain static. Customer patterns, layouts, camera conditions, and other factors change over time.

To cope with that drift, the researchers developed a periodic adaptation framework that learns from new, unlabeled data collected at the site rather than leaving the model frozen after initial training. Earlier work from the group similarly explored continual learning for anomaly-detection systems operating in changing environments.

That matters because “normal” is not permanent.

The approach also changes what the analytics layer needs to know about the people being observed. “We don’t do any facial recognition, and we don’t use any personally identifiable information,” Tabkhi said. “We are blind with respect to those details.”

Pose-based anomaly detection replaces much of a person’s visual appearance with information about body position and movement. The researchers argue that this can both reduce privacy exposure and limit appearance-related biases that can enter pixel-based systems.

For example, a person wearing different clothing from everyone around them should not be considered anomalous if that person is moving normally. Removing clothing, facial features, and other appearance information allows the model to concentrate more directly on behavior.

AI as an attention mechanism

An anomaly does not necessarily mean a crime has occurred. A group suddenly dancing in a coffee shop, for example, would probably violate the system’s expectations. That makes it unusual, not dangerous. Tabkhi therefore does not want the AI to make the final judgment.

“AI is not a decision-maker,” he said. “AI rather is an attention mechanism to enhance and scale human cognition across many cameras.”

When the system flags behavior, a human operator can examine the original CCTV footage and decide whether anything requires action. Tabkhi acknowledged that false positives and false negatives cannot be eliminated, making fully automated security decisions inappropriate.

Tabkhi’s group also developed ALFred, an active-learning framework for semi-supervised video anomaly detection that brings human feedback into the learning loop. The system selects uncertain or informative examples for human review, then uses that feedback to refine anomaly labels and adjust detection thresholds as conditions change.

The objective is not to replace the security operator but to reduce the impossible task of expecting people to watch large numbers of camera feeds continuously.

That changes the fundamental question that security AI asks. Instead of always trying to determine, “What threat am I looking at?”, Tabkhi’s work increasingly asks something closer to: “Given what has happened so far, what should happen next?”

If reality breaks the learned pattern, a human gets a chance to look. That may be the most useful language for intelligent cameras to learn.

Nvidia has acquired HuggingFace for $12.9 billion. The startup, which is named after an emoji, was founded by three French entrepreneurs in 2016. It has become the go-to repository for open-source AI models, datasets, and associated software libraries.

In a press conference announcing the deal, Nvidia VP of AI software Justin Boitano was faced with many questions about the neutrality of HuggingFace’s offering.

“We’re committed to helping build this community, stewarding, and fostering this community, Boitano said. “We want to continue to work with all AI developers globally to make sure that they’ve got an open and neutral platform that interoperates with every cloud provider, every hardware company in the world.”

Nvidia believes in maintaining a healthy ecosystem of closed model providers and open models, he added, noting that open models give companies the ability to build their own domain-specific intelligence. Nvidia is by far HuggingFace’s biggest contributor.

Boitano said that it’s in Nvidia’s interests to keep HuggingFace hardware-neutral.

“The Hugging Face team has built an amazing community, […] and the only way you do that is by building the trust of the developer community and giving developers access to run the models and access the datasets from any platform in the world that they want to run it on,” he said. “We are incentivized and motivated to keep this open and neutral and ensure that developers can work wherever they want to work, accessing and connecting the best open models into and across every cloud provider, every neocloud, and into every data center and make availability on every device.”

Nvidia-specific runtimes will continue to exist alongside open-source runtimes such as vLLM and SGLang, which are open and neutral, ensuring all open models in the HuggingFace repository can be optimized for all hardware, Boitano said.

HuggingFace co-founder and CEO Clem Delangue said that the acquisition would still mean all the players in today’s ecosystem can use open-source foundations to build whatever they want.

“The vast majority of what we do is open source—open models, open datasets that are by definition neutral—everyone can take them, everyone can optimize them, everyone can fork our open source if they’re not happy about it,” he said. “Almost by definition, everything that we do is open and neutral and gives everyone the capabilities to build more.”

Delangue, who is French, shot down a suggestion that the acquisition of HuggingFace was emblematic of the difficulties of building tech giants in the EU.

“All three co-founders are French, but I was already in the U.S. when we started the company, so quite naturally, we built it with American investors,” he said. “I think it’s going to create really positive effects on the European tech ecosystem because obviously the founders are French, a big part of the team is French, and so we hope that after this acquisition, they’ll be able to reinvest quite a lot in the European tech ecosystem.”

HuggingFace will continue to support open models and open datasets from around the globe, and Delangue said he hopes to include more open models out of European labs such as Mistral in France and Black Forest Labs in Germany.

Delangue said that the HuggingFace team is excited to now have the ability to “think long-term.” Nvidia’s support will enable HuggingFace to reach its goal of 100 million builders on the platform much more quickly, he said, noting that the platform has around 18 million users today.

“We think we’re at the inflection point for HuggingFace and for open-source AI in general,” he said. “We think with the resources, with the support, with the long-term approach of Nvidia, we’ll be able to do basically what we’ve been doing for the past 10 years, meaning, supporting the open-source AI community, but to the next level at a much bigger scale, which we think is really needed for the field and for the world.”

data.title: Kioxia’s Flash-for-DRAM Initiative Eyes AI Workloads
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Kioxia has moved one step closer to its ambitious goal of replacing DRAM with flash for some memory content serving AI workloads. It presented a Compute Express Link (CXL) module at a briefing in Tokyo; the module is built around XL-Flash, a specialized NAND chip with sharply improved processing speeds.

This CXL module—aimed at replacing part of DRAM content alongside AI compute—uses NAND flash optimized for high-speed processing. Kioxia claims that replacing some DRAM with CXL modules can double memory capacity at the same cost while improving performance by 30%.

CXL—an interface standard that ties together different memory types and devices inside a system into a single large memory space—allows capacity to be allocated dynamically as needed. As a result, a NAND-based CXL module is cost-competitive against DRAM. While DRAM reads data extremely fast, it is difficult to expand in capacity and is more expensive.

On the other hand, cheaper NAND-based CXL enables an ultra-large memory pool at a lower cost than a DRAM-only configuration. Here, substituting NAND for DRAM in certain AI workloads hinges on evolving system architectures that can tolerate higher latency in exchange for greater density and lower cost per bit.

Flash window of opportunity

NAND flash offers substantially more storage capacity at a given price point, but its access speeds are measured in microseconds rather than DRAM’s nanoseconds. However, emerging applications in data center tiering and edge AI now provide new openings for systems designed to manage mixed-latency storage hierarchies.

These systems can route less time-sensitive operations to flash-based memory while reserving DRAM for performance-critical tasks. Consider machine learning (ML) model inference in data center environments, where latency may not matter much unless it’s more than an order of magnitude worse than high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

Next, in edge AI, which commonly employs pre-trained models, Kioxia’s CXL module aligns with NAND’s advantage of large capacity. It’s also immune to NAND’s weaknesses of slow writes and limited endurance, and its low-power consumption suits energy-sensitive edge environments.

At this memory-technology crossroads, a CXL module can boost NAND flash memory processing speeds as part of the initiative to replace some DRAM demand in AI servers. Consequently, if NAND can absorb some DRAM capacity in data center servers and emerging applications such as edge AI, the addressable market for flash widens at the expense of DRAM chips.

Nevertheless, Kioxia’s flash-for-DRAM initiative is a supplementary strategy rather than a core design initiative. It heeds specialized NAND applications that can offset the absence of DRAM. But the question is: why Kioxia?

Kioxia’s memory imperative

Unlike other top-tier memory producers—Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix—Kioxia lacks a DRAM portfolio. That leaves the Japanese memory chipmaker exposed in a market where its key rivals can leverage both DRAM and flash memory technologies. In other words, Kioxia’s singular focus on NAND flash has become a liability.

Moreover, within the NAND flash space, China’s Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. (YMTC) is narrowing the multi-year technology gap in a matter of months. That especially threatens Kioxia’s position in price-sensitive memory segments. Then there is Micron, which has regained momentum in the NAND flash market after a difficult stretch spanning many years.

Such competitive pressures have left Kioxia searching for strategic differentiation. Here, it must extract value from its existing NAND capabilities through novel initiatives: enter the NAND-based CXL module to replace some DRAM demand. But that’s only half of the story.

In NAND-based CXL module design, while technical tradeoffs are well understood, implementation requires software stacks and system designs that exploit the cost-density advantages while managing latency penalties. That, in turn, calls for ecosystem support from server manufacturers, hyperscalers, and software vendors.

Without design wins and ecosystem support, it will remain a forward-looking statement regarding memory architecture rather than a memory industry breakthrough. Therefore, industry watchers are keenly awaiting design win announcements from Kioxia; they will validate the technical premise of NAND substitution in memory-intensive AI workloads.

Until then, Kioxia carving out a middle path to position flash as a tier between DRAM and storage will remain a work in progress. While the technical details of this unlaunched module are making waves in the memory world, flash as a DRAM proxy must open a differentiated revenue stream to become a persistent HBM twin.

Summer is usually quiet in the U.K. and most of Europe, with a majority of people taking annual vacation for a few weeks. Against this backdrop, it was refreshing to see over 700 semiconductor industry executives gather at a one-day conference in London for the first TechWorks Semiconductors to Systems Summit (S2S26).

At the event, TechWorks also announced that several different communities that had evolved from the National Microelectronics Institute (NMI), formed in 1996, are to come together under a single umbrella, the UK Semiconductor Industry Association, or UKSIA. TechWorks CEO Charles Sturman told EE Times that the UKSIA will create a unified industry body to advocate for the sector, streamline government dialogue, and help secure funding and policy support across the domestic semiconductor value chain. He was keen to emphasize that it would still sit alongside the automotive electronics and cybersecurity groups, namely AESIN and IoTSF.

Sturman said, “The key here is that while semiconductors [are] all pervasive, there are organizations in aerospace, defense, cybersecurity, and so on where semiconductors [are] not their focus, but they have interest in it. So, groups like AESIN and IoTSF will continue for now to be communities focused on specific interests, sitting alongside UKSIA. The UKSIA is focused on supporting our semiconductor industry members. It is a natural partner to the UK Semiconductor Centre (UKSC), a publicly funded organization that speaks for national interest.”

He added, “By aligning closely with UKSC, UKSIA and our members get a single, coherent route into the roadmaps, programs, and international relationships that UKSC is building, and it gives UKSC a credible industry counterpart.”

EE Times caught up with Sturman to get a sense of what the S2S26 event meant in the wider global context. You can watch the full video interview here:

You can also listen to the audio-only version of the interview here:

S2S26 reflects a buzz in chip industry

According to data EE Times pulled from Tracxn this week, U.K. semiconductor companies raised approximately $432.9 million in 2026 so far, from Jan. 1 through Sept. 3. This represents a 65% rise in just eight months, compared to the full year of 2025, when U.K. companies raised $262.3 million in total.

Last week’s S2S26 event in London was clearly a reflection of this buzz in the U.K, and signaled two things: the broader excitement we are seeing across the semiconductor industry worldwide, with participants eager to attend events that enable them to build and strengthen relationships within the highly interconnected networks of the semiconductor ecosystem; and secondly, something the U.K. needed: a single event to bring together the different groups that have evolved over the years, including TechWorks NMI, DESN, AESIN, and IoT Security Foundation communities, supported by the newly established UK Semiconductor Centre (see our interview with UKSC CEO Andy McLean).

It’s interesting to note that the U.K. still has other events that are thriving, such as Hardware Pioneers Max and the more recently launched Microelectronics U.K.

The TechWorks S2S26 event, which featured four different tracks—appropriately named build, create, secure, and scale—also marked the industry group’s 30th anniversary, as it evolved from the National Microelectronics Institute (NMI). Reflecting the global interconnectedness of the chip industry, the event also involved international partners from Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, and Germany.

According to its press announcement, TechWorks said: “The scale of S2S26 reflects a U.K. deep-tech sector that is becoming increasingly interconnected, as technologies including semiconductors, AI, photonics, advanced packaging, electronic systems, and cybersecurity converge across industries.”  Topics ranged from next-generation semiconductor materials, GaN power semiconductors, and photonics to AI-enabled manufacturing, advanced packaging, chiplets, digital twins, autonomous systems, electrification, and post-quantum security.

In an interview with EE Times, Sturman said the aim of the event was to bridge the gaps between early-stage device materials research, silicon design, software co-development, and final system integration. The summit highlighted four main operational tracks addressing the full lifecycle of modern technology stack design, from advanced manufacturing and packaging down to software-defined architectures and investment pathways.

Sturman’s remarks in the organization’s formal post-show announcement probably summed it up best. He said, “The response to S2S26 demonstrates the extraordinary level of ambition and capability that exists across U.K. deep tech. What was particularly striking was the sense of common purpose: People want to work together, and there is real confidence about what the U.K. can achieve. S2S26 showed what can happen when we stop looking at individual technologies and sectors in isolation and start connecting the whole ecosystem. The challenge now is to maintain that momentum.”

data.title: India’s Quantum Journey Goes Beyond the Qubit
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

India is getting access to one of the world’s most advanced quantum computing platforms while trying to build its own quantum hardware industry.

IBM’s planned Quantum System Two installation in Amaravati, Andhra Pradesh, will put a production quantum system within reach of Indian researchers and startups, even as companies such as QpiAI work on indigenous processors, control electronics, and software. That creates an unusual opportunity for India’s quantum program: The country does not have to wait for domestic processors to mature before developing algorithms, applications, and quantum engineering capabilities.

Globally, quantum computing is still far from being a conventional enterprise computing market. IBM’s global quantum network includes more than 325 organizations, but most use IBM’s quantum machines for research and intellectual property development rather than to deploy enterprise quantum applications.

India’s national quantum policy

India’s National Quantum Mission (NQM) has approved a ₹6,003.65 crore (~$626.8 million) outlay over eight years to build the quantum infrastructure in India while expanding support to quantum startups working on processors, sensing, communications, and quantum-safe technologies.

The NQM has established four thematic hubs covering quantum computing, communications, sensing, and metrology, as well as quantum materials and devices. Of ₹2,330.68 crore (~$243.3 million) sanctioned across the four thematic hubs through March 2031, the mission has so far released ₹699.5 crore (~$73.02 million).

(Editor’s note: USD amounts in this section are per the conversion rates in August 2026.)

The hubs, hosted by IISc Bengaluru, IIT Madras, with C-DoT, IIT Bombay, and IIT Delhi, became operational in the 2024–2025 financial year, each as a Section 8 company with its own governing board. The NQM has also expanded support to nine startups, taking the total to 17. The new ventures are working in quantum biosensors, photon sensing, quantum positioning, atomic memory, and precision electronics.

The mission’s technology targets give a rough measure of the scale that India expects its indigenous quantum computing capabilities to reach: 20 to 50 physical qubits within three years, 50 to 100 within five years, and 50 to 1,000 within eight years. Those targets are below the qubit counts of IBM’s current systems, although qubit count alone does not determine a quantum system’s performance. Circuit depth, error rates, and connectivity also matter, as Amith Singhee, CTO of IBM India and South Asia, told EE Times.

The mission’s progress is already visible outside quantum computing. India has demonstrated a 1,000-km quantum key distribution network in less than two years, reaching half of the mission’s eight-year target of 2,000 km. The network uses indigenous technology developed by QNu Labs, which the Department of Science and Technology identifies as a startup supported under the NQM.

Why IBM wants to be in India

Singhee explained that useful quantum computing is not simply a matter of installing a machine but of building a network of users.

“One is the technology stack, hardware and software [to make useful quantum computing],” he said. “But the second part, which is equally, if not more, important, is to have a network of users who use the thing and tell us what is working, what is not working, but also use the thing to advance the application algorithms layer. Without that feedback loop, the system is just a piece of metal.”

That feedback loop is central to IBM’s rationale for the Amaravati installation. Singhee said India’s academic research groups, startups, and established companies are creating enough momentum for IBM to engage with the ecosystem while quantum applications are still taking shape.

The choice of Amaravati, according to Singhee, was driven less by the availability of a particular facility and more by the Andhra Pradesh government’s effort to bring together companies, researchers, and government agencies around the technology. IBM, TATA Consultancy Services, Larsen & Toubro, the Department of Science and Technology, and IIT were among the organizations involved in early discussions about building the ecosystem.

Undefined by qubits

Quantum System Two is IBM’s system architecture rather than a fixed processor generation. IBM’s original announcement of the Amaravati deployment said the system would feature a 156-qubit Heron processor. Singhee clarified that the quantum processing unit (QPU) ultimately installed will be whichever processor is production-ready when IBM begins shipping and assembling the system. “I would not say it is necessarily Heron,” he said.

Heron has been IBM’s flagship processor, with 133- and 156-qubit versions. Nighthawk, unveiled by IBM at its Quantum Developer Conference in November 2025, is the next processor in the pipeline. Singhee said that Nighthawk is designed to push the noise floor lower and allow deeper, more complex circuits.

Singhee also pushed back on treating qubit count alone as a measure of capability. “A processor might have 300 physical qubits but only 120 programmable qubits,” he said. He stressed that qubit count needs to be considered along with circuit depth, 2-qubit error rates, operation speed, and connectivity.

Infrastructure behind a QPU

A quantum computer is not a server that gets bolted into a data center rack. Singhee described the facility requirement as being closer to scientific equipment than a conventional data center, with a roughly 100-square-meter room with power, temperature control, and water infrastructure, centered on a dilution refrigerator that cools the quantum processor to about 10 to 20 millikelvins. The refrigerator uses a mixture of helium-3 and helium-4 to reach those temperatures.

Inside the dilution refrigerator, the QPU sits at the coldest stage, surrounded by the cryogenic wiring, filtering, and amplification needed to control and measure the qubits. Singhee described the assembly as “chandelier-like,” referring to the stacked cooling stages and dense network of signal lines that connect the QPU to electronics outside the refrigerator. Microwave pulses travel down these lines to control the superconducting qubits, while extremely weak readout signals travel back through the cryogenic system and are amplified by low-noise amplifiers before reaching room-temperature electronics for digitization and processing.

IBM assembles and manages the full system but does not build every component itself. “We do not necessarily build all of the cryogenic electronics,” Singhee said, adding that IBM has suppliers for components such as dilution refrigerators and cryogenic electronics. Some components may be delivered directly to India, while others are pre-integrated in the U.S. before being shipped to India for final assembly.

That supply chain also creates opportunities for India beyond the processor itself. “Why aren’t dilution refrigerators made in India?” Singhee said, pointing to cryogenic electronics, wiring, dilution refrigerators, and other peripherals used in quantum systems. He also cited India’s engineering base and government initiatives, including Make in India, the RDI Fund, and the semiconductor mission, as factors that could help build capacity in these areas.

While the infrastructure required to operate a superconducting quantum computer is specialized, Singhee does not see cryogenics as the primary barrier to scaling quantum systems. The harder problems are reaching large numbers of logical qubits, connecting processors, and reducing the overhead of error correction.

“Real-world workloads could eventually require millions of physical qubits,” Singhee said. Current processors operate at roughly 100 to 150 qubits and could eventually reach about 1,000 qubits on a chip.

Moving from individual chips to much larger systems introduces a quantum networking problem. Qubits on different chips would need to be connected in a way that allows them to operate as part of a larger quantum system. Multiple chips also cannot simply be placed in a single dilution refrigerator indefinitely, creating another connectivity challenge between quantum systems.

Error correction adds another layer. Quantum processors require additional qubits and circuitry to detect and correct errors, but the overhead can become large enough to make fault-tolerant systems impractical unless more efficient error-correction codes and lower-overhead hardware implementations are developed.

That distinction is important for India because increasing physical qubit counts on indigenous processors is only one part of the longer-term hardware problem. The industry ultimately must turn those physical qubits into sufficiently reliable logical qubits that can run useful workloads.

QpiAI’s indigenous quantum effort

The NQM’s targets, however, are not just policy milestones. Indian startups are already trying to build the hardware needed to reach them.

QpiAI inaugurated its Quantum Foundry in Bengaluru, the first facility of its kind in India. The startup claims that it is Asia’s largest quantum foundry, forming part of a 70,000-square-foot R&D center that brings together QPU manufacturing, testing, and quantum solution development under one roof.

The facility will manufacture superconducting qubits, peripheral chips, and sensors for quantum computers and can fabricate flip-chip-based superconducting qubits of up to 128 qubits, with the next phase scheduled for 2027, targeting up to 10,000 physical qubits on a single QPU.

The Bengaluru-based startup, founded by Nagendra Nagaraja, has already fabricated four quantum processors: the 8-qubit QVidya, 25-qubit Indus, and 64-qubit Kaveri, all based on transmon qubits, along with the 9-qubit Yukti, built on its own variation of fluxonium technology. It also has a roadmap running through its 128-qubit Emuna, 256-qubit Ganges, and 1,000-qubit Everest systems. In parallel, it is developing logical qubits: QpiAI is targeting 100 logical qubits by around 2029, a threshold that Nagaraja said would make quantum computing viable for large-scale commercial deployment.

QpiAI designed its own controller in-house. “We designed our own proprietary controller rather than sourcing one from the market, as it integrates tightly with our AI software, which tunes the qubits,” Nagaraja told EE Times in an earlier interaction. The controller operates across a wide frequency range, generating and reading the microwave pulses that drive the qubits, with extensive filtering built into both the FPGA and the board to strip out noise before it reaches the processor.

QpiAI outsources PCB design and, for now, sources some board components from Singapore and Taiwan, though Nagaraja said the company is working with Indian manufacturers to bring specialized board production onshore.

Nagaraja chose superconducting qubits over neutral-atom or ion-trap approaches for reasons that echo, without directly citing, IBM’s own architecture choice. “Superconducting qubits are solid-state devices, making them ideal for integration into data centers,” he said, arguing that gas chambers and lasers used in competing qubit technologies have unproven long-term reliability in a data center environment.

Research comes before enterprise deployment

Singhee said he expects Amaravati’s earliest work to cluster around computational chemistry, materials science, optimization, and machine learning, with production-scale enterprise use still some years away.

The first value of the system may therefore be less about running production workloads than about giving Indian researchers hands-on experience with hardware that remains difficult to access.

Where the two systems might eventually intersect is at the software layer. Singhee raised the possibility of a common programming interface that could run across different quantum hardware, similar to how Linux runs across chips from different vendors, with IBM’s Qiskit as one candidate.

QpiAI’s own stack—hardware, system software, compilers, libraries, and applications—is built to be self-contained rather than interoperable with outside hardware today, but Nagaraja’s answers point toward the same eventual layering: a controller and software stack that can be adapted as the underlying processors scale.

QpiAI has since also moved to open its own software layer as well, releasing the QpiAI Quantum SDK as open-source, giving developers a Python-based toolkit for circuit creation, simulation, and algorithm development that connects to QpiAI’s 8-qubit and 25-qubit systems through its QCloud platform. Unlike Qiskit, however, the SDK is currently scoped to QpiAI’s own hardware rather than functioning as a cross-vendor interface.

Singhee compared the possible future programming layer to Linux, where the same operating system can run across processors from different vendors. IBM is already examining whether Qiskit can work with other quantum hardware platforms, creating a potential path for Indian hardware developers to participate in a broader software ecosystem.

“Definitely our Qiskit platform is a promising candidate,” Singhee said. “We are working with one or two other hardware vendors who have their own hardware to see how Qiskit can work with their hardware. That would be an interesting synergy point also for the Indian hardware developers.”

The model also reflects how IBM expects quantum computers to be used in practice. Quantum processors are unlikely to replace classical computers. Instead, they are expected to operate alongside classical computing and AI, with each handling the parts of a workload suited to its capabilities.

For example, Singhee described molecular simulation workflows in which classical computing, potentially assisted by AI, estimates a molecule’s geometry before the problem is mapped onto a quantum processor. The quantum system generates possible electronic states, and those results are returned to classical computing to update the model. The process can be repeated until the calculation converges.

That hybrid model makes the surrounding software, classical infrastructure, and algorithms part of the quantum computing stack. For India, the opportunity therefore extends beyond building processors to developing applications, engineering capabilities, and the talent needed to use them.

“We hope and expect that India will become a major player in quantum software and services at the least,” Singhee said. “There is going to be a big global market in quantum over the next decade or so. India should capture half of it just like it has in the enterprise software and services sector.”

Building that capability will require skills extending beyond quantum physics. “We have been growing our quantum team at IBM in India for the last four years or so,” Singhee said. “These are people who have master’s [degrees] or Ph.D.’s in quantum information science; they understand the fundamentals and how algorithms work to engage our collaborators.

“We also hire software engineers with a strong math background to develop the programming layer like Qiskit and so on,” he added.

That mix of quantum expertise, software engineering, and hardware development points to the broader challenge for India’s quantum program. The country can gain access to advanced processors before it can build comparable systems itself, but turning that access into a domestic industry calls for the ability to develop around the processor at the same time.

IBM’s Amaravati system can provide researchers with access to advanced hardware now while QpiAI and other startups work on domestic processors and the NQM builds research infrastructure. The longer-term test is whether those efforts develop into a connected ecosystem of hardware, software, applications, suppliers, and talent rather than remaining separate parts of India’s quantum program.

Automotive functional safety chiplet startup Athos Silicon has closed its doors.

Former Athos CEO Charnjiv Bangar told EE Times that Athos has ceased operations after its board made the decision to wind down and dissolve the company.

“Despite extensive efforts, we were unable to secure the financing required to continue the productization and commercialization of our technology,” Bangar said. “This was not a decision we made lightly. The technology was consistently well received by the technical community and prospective partners with whom we engaged. Ultimately, the challenge was financial and cap-table related rather than technical, and the board made its decision on the company’s financing position.”

Athos had spun out of Mercedes-Benz after five years of incubation, with Mercedes making a strategic investment that included substantial IP. The team had been addressing functional safety for autonomous driving and other autonomy applications with a new architecture that combined multiple chiplets to offer a level of redundancy in case of hardware failures. Key to the architecture is a patented voting mechanism that enables chiplets to monitor their neighbors for failures. The architecture also includes techniques for moving workloads between chiplets to provide uninterrupted service in the event of a failure.

Athos originally developed its architecture around purchasing and integrating third-party chiplets, including DreamBig’s chiplet hub, but redrew its roadmap following the acquisition of DreamBig by Arm. The new plan had been to tape out Athos’s own SoC chiplet using third-party IP, using multiples of a single tape-out on an organic substrate to keep costs down.

The startup had been targeting autonomous driving in the long term and small autonomous systems such as drones in the near term with a single-chiplet version of the design.

Under the licensing agreement with Mercedes-Benz, the original IP licensed from Mercedes has reverted back to them. IP developed after the spinout remains with its inventors, Bangar said.

data.title: Manufacturing Growth Slows in August Amid Supply and Cost Strains
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Economic activity in the U.S. manufacturing sector expanded in August for the eighth consecutive month. However, momentum slowed from July’s multi-year peak as order growth cooled, backlogs shrank, and persistent supply chain bottlenecks kept cost pressures high.

The Institute for Supply Management reported that its Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index, or PMI, was 54.6% in August, down 1 percentage point from July’s 55.6%. While this shows a slowdown from the prior month’s four-year high, it remained well above the 50% threshold separating expansion from contraction. This signals the general economy expanded for its 22nd month in a row. Historically, a Manufacturing PMI of 54.6% corresponds to an annualized 2.4% increase in real gross domestic product, down from the 2.8% pace in July.

“In August, U.S. manufacturing activity remained in expansion territory, though it has lost ground in a number of key measures—namely, the New Orders, Backlog, and Imports indexes,” said Susan Spence, chair of the ISM Manufacturing Business Survey Committee. “Of the five subindexes that make up the PMI, the only one that grew faster than last month was Supplier Deliveries (up 0.4 percentage point), indicating a continuing slowdown of the supply chain.”

Factory output and new orders slow

Output across American factory floors continued to advance in August but at a slower pace following July’s surge. The ISM Production Index fell 0.2 percentage points to 58.3%, maintaining expansion for the 10th consecutive month. Four of the nation’s six largest industrial sectors—Petroleum & Coal Products, Transportation Equipment, Machinery, and Chemical Products—reported output gains. However, the ratio of positive-to-negative comments about output dropped to 2.2-to-1 from 3.3-to-1 in July.

Demand indicators also showed cooler sentiment. The New Orders Index registered 53.7%, down 3 percentage points from July’s 56.7%. While new bookings expanded for the eighth straight month, demand sentiment weakened, with a 2-to-1 ratio of positive to negative remarks compared with 3.5-to-1 in July. At the same time, the Backlog of Orders Index fell 3.2 percentage points to 51.8%, and the Imports Index dropped 3.2 percentage points to 52.5%.

Much of the core manufacturing momentum remains concentrated around semiconductors, data center buildouts, and defense manufacturing, even as broader industrial demand wobbles. “Photonics, high-speed connectors, semiconductors, and government orders are expanding significantly,” said an executive in the machinery industry. “Supply chains domestically and globally are difficult, with increases in lead times and cost.”

A supply executive in the computer and electronic products sector described an increasingly intricate operating backdrop: “Supply chain situation, especially in the electronics market, is going through another crisis even bigger and more complicated than during and post Covid-19. That’s mainly due to AI infrastructure and uncertainties in the global market (for oil and other critical supplies) due to war in the Middle East and more complication on trade rules.”

Slow hiring as companies adjust headcounts

Factory payrolls grew for the second consecutive month in August, but hiring activity slowed as producers carefully balanced staffing against easing order backlogs. The ISM Employment Index registered 51.2%, down 1.6 percentage points from 52.8% in July.

Labor market adjustments among manufacturers showed growing caution. “Of the six big manufacturing industries, only Transportation Equipment reported higher levels of employment in August,” Spence noted. “The panelist comment ratio of hiring to managing/reducing headcounts was 1.3-to-1,” sliding from the 1.5-to-1 in July. Among the 18 surveyed industries, seven expanded their workforce, three reduced headcounts, and eight kept employment unchanged.

Producers also noted structural operational shifts amid trade pressures. “Volume is consistent,” said an executive in the transportation equipment sector. “Our main customer is shifting production from U.S. plants to Mexico.” Another panelist warned of rising tariff costs: “High steel and aluminum prices (due to Section 232 tariffs) continue to make profitability a challenge. Uncertainty over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement is at the forefront of many customer conversations. Our industry has also been hit with countervailing and anti-dumping penalties, further raising the cost of equipment.”

Inflation due to the Iran war and other geopolitical friction impacts production

While demand and employment moderated, industrial input costs remained high. The ISM Prices Index was 71.1% in August, matching July and showing raw material costs rose for the 23rd consecutive month. Higher commodity prices were reported by 46.2% of respondents, down from 50.2% in July, though 15 of 18 industries still paid higher input prices.

“The Prices Index reading is still being driven by (1) increases in steel and aluminum prices that impact the entire value chain, (2) tariffs applied to many imported goods, and (3) increases in petroleum-based products as a result of the Middle East conflict,” Spence said.

Supply logistics tightened further in August, with the Supplier Deliveries Index rising 0.4 percentage points to 59.3%, marking slower deliveries for the ninth consecutive month. Panelist sentiment was cautious: 58% of comments were negative versus 42% positive, a 1-to-1.4 ratio. Pricing volatility was the main concern, cited in 57% of negative responses, followed by longer lead times at 46%, the war in Iran at 30%, and tariffs at 29%.

In the primary metals sector, an executive remarked on acute market opacity: “This month is a blur: Steel prices continue to climb as supply diminishes, aluminum is rising after dropping, and there are many holes on the plate side. Demand seems to be a seesaw. Our prediction ability continues to diminish, with the exception that the year will remain difficult until the end.”

Divergent trends across manufacturing sectors

Despite growing macro headwinds, 15 of the 18 manufacturing industries tracked by the ISM posted growth in August, led by Primary Metals; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; and Miscellaneous Manufacturing. Five of the nation’s six largest industrial sectors expanded, with Chemical Products joining Wood Products as the only two industries reporting outright contraction.

Even with broad industry growth, signals of stress widened slightly across the industrial base. Approximately 22% of manufacturing gross domestic product contracted in August, compared with 20% in July, and 2% of manufacturing GDP fell into strong contraction—defined as a composite PMI of 45% or lower—up from zero in July.
